external_prereqs: how cyclones form over warm oceans

misconceptions.statement: Standing in a doorway is the safest place during an earthquake.
misconceptions.why: Old advice and pictures of doorframes surviving in old mud-brick houses spread widely.
misconceptions.fix: Modern doorframes are not stronger than the walls and doors can swing and hit you. Drop, cover under a sturdy table and hold on.

probe.question: Shaking starts in your classroom with a desk nearby. Where is it safest to go?

misconceptions.root_belief: old folk advice must be true
misconceptions.source_hint: disaster-management agency guidance debunking the doorway myth

misconceptions.statement: During an earthquake you should run outside as fast as possible.
misconceptions.why: People instinctively want to leave a shaking building.
misconceptions.fix: Running during shaking risks falls and falling debris. Drop, cover and hold on until shaking stops, then leave calmly.

probe.question: The floor shakes while you are inside. What do you do first?
probe.wrong_answer: Run out of the building immediately.

misconceptions.root_belief: escaping is always safer than staying
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of earthquake behaviour and injuries

misconceptions.statement: Drop, Cover, Hold On is useless because a building will fall anyway.
misconceptions.why: Images of collapsed buildings make protection seem hopeless.
misconceptions.fix: Most injuries come from falling objects and flying items. Covering under a sturdy table greatly reduces them.

probe.question: Why do we take cover under a table in an earthquake?
probe.wrong_answer: It does not help; the building falls anyway.

misconceptions.root_belief: big disasters cannot be survived by small actions

misconceptions.statement: Standing under a tree or near a building outside is safe during a quake.
misconceptions.why: Students think anything open or sturdy-looking is safe.
misconceptions.fix: Move to an open area away from buildings, wires and trees. Falling glass, bricks and poles are dangerous.

probe.question: You are in a street during shaking. Where should you stand?
probe.wrong_answer: Next to a tall building wall.

misconceptions.root_belief: solid-looking things are always safe

misconceptions.statement: A lift is the quickest and safest way down during an earthquake.
misconceptions.why: Lifts are the normal fast way to leave tall buildings.
misconceptions.fix: Power can fail and the lift can get stuck. Use the stairs after shaking stops.

probe.question: You are on the 5th floor after shaking stops. How should you go down?

misconceptions.root_belief: a normal habit works in emergencies

misconceptions.statement: Standing near a window lets you see and escape quickly during shaking.
misconceptions.why: Students think visibility and an exit make a spot safe.
misconceptions.fix: Windows can shatter and cause cuts. Stay away from glass, heavy shelves and hanging objects.

probe.question: Which spot is worse in a classroom during an earthquake: under a desk or next to a window?
probe.wrong_answer: Next to the window is better.

misconceptions.root_belief: being near an exit means being safe

misconceptions.statement: Once the main earthquake is over, there is no more danger.
misconceptions.why: People assume a single event ends when shaking stops.
misconceptions.fix: Aftershocks can follow for hours or days and can damage weakened buildings. Stay alert and keep away from damaged structures.

probe.question: The strong shaking stopped. Is it safe to go back inside a cracked building?

misconceptions.root_belief: one event is a single moment
misconceptions.source_hint: seismology and disaster education literature on aftershocks

misconceptions.statement: After a quake you should light a match or candle to check for gas leaks.
misconceptions.why: Students think fire lets you see and smell better in the dark.
misconceptions.fix: Never use flames or switches near a suspected leak. Open windows, turn off the gas and leave.

probe.question: You smell gas after shaking. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Light a candle to look around.

misconceptions.root_belief: light helps in dark situations always

misconceptions.statement: Floods only happen where it is raining heavily at that place.
misconceptions.why: Students link a flood only to local rain.
misconceptions.fix: Rain far upstream, dam releases or tidal surges can flood places that are dry at that time.

probe.question: It is sunny in your town but the river upstream got heavy rain. Can your town flood?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is not raining here.

misconceptions.root_belief: effects happen only where the cause is
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about floods and the water cycle

misconceptions.statement: If the flood warning is issued, you can wait until water enters your house before leaving.
misconceptions.why: Students think danger only starts when water reaches them.
misconceptions.fix: Water can rise fast. Move to high ground or shelter as soon as the warning is given.

probe.question: A flood warning is announced for your village. When should you leave?

misconceptions.root_belief: danger begins only when it reaches me

misconceptions.statement: Shallow, slow-moving floodwater is safe to walk or drive through.
misconceptions.why: Students judge danger by how deep or fast water looks.
misconceptions.fix: Just 15 cm of fast water can knock a person down and 30 cm can float a car. Hidden holes and currents make it dangerous.

probe.question: A road is covered in knee-deep water. Should you cross it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it looks calm so it is safe.

misconceptions.root_belief: small or calm-looking means harmless
misconceptions.source_hint: flood-safety studies on fatalities from driving or walking through water

misconceptions.statement: Electricity is only dangerous if wires are visibly sparking in floodwater.
misconceptions.why: Students expect electricity hazards to be visible.
misconceptions.fix: Water conducts electricity and fallen or submerged wires can electrify water without any sign. Stay away and switch off the mains if safe.

probe.question: A wire is in floodwater but not sparking. Is it safe to wade nearby?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on invisible hazards in electrical safety education

misconceptions.statement: Floodwater is clean because it is rainwater.
misconceptions.why: Students associate rain with pure water.
misconceptions.fix: Floodwater mixes with sewage, chemicals and waste, so it carries germs. Avoid contact and wash well afterward.

probe.question: Is it safe to play in clear-looking floodwater?

misconceptions.root_belief: clear-looking water is clean
misconceptions.source_hint: public health guidance and studies on waterborne disease after floods

misconceptions.statement: Clear water from a flooded area is safe to drink without boiling.
misconceptions.why: Students judge water safety by appearance.
misconceptions.fix: Germs cannot be seen. Boil water for at least a minute, or use chlorine tablets or bottled water.

probe.question: Flood water has settled and looks clear. Can you drink it?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about water purity

misconceptions.statement: When the calm eye of a cyclone arrives, the storm is over and you can go outside.
misconceptions.why: The weather suddenly turns clear and calm.
misconceptions.fix: The eye is short, and violent winds return from the opposite side. Stay inside until officials say it is safe.

probe.question: Winds suddenly stop and the sky clears during a cyclone. What do you do?

misconceptions.root_belief: calm conditions mean danger has ended
misconceptions.source_hint: meteorological education research and disaster agency reports on the eye

misconceptions.statement: A strong house means you need not go to a cyclone shelter.
misconceptions.why: Students trust their own home and fear leaving it.
misconceptions.fix: Only buildings designed to resist cyclones are safe. If authorities order evacuation, go to the shelter early.

probe.question: Evacuation is ordered but your house looks strong. What do you do?

misconceptions.root_belief: my own place is safest

misconceptions.statement: You can wait to go to the shelter until the cyclone hits.
misconceptions.why: Students underestimate the time needed to travel safely in the storm.
misconceptions.fix: Roads become unsafe once winds start. Move to the shelter as soon as the warning is issued.

probe.question: A cyclone is expected tomorrow. When do you go to the shelter?

misconceptions.root_belief: danger begins only when it reaches me

misconceptions.statement: Strong wind is the main cause of cyclone deaths.
misconceptions.why: Students notice wind most in news pictures.
misconceptions.fix: Storm surge, a rise of sea water onto land, causes most deaths near coasts. Move away from the coast.

probe.question: What is the biggest danger to people on the coast during a cyclone?

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: cyclone mortality studies and IMD/NDMA reports

misconceptions.statement: Storm surge is the same as a normal high tide.
misconceptions.why: Both involve the sea rising.
misconceptions.fix: Storm surge is a rise caused by cyclone winds and low pressure, and can be several metres above normal tide.

probe.question: How is a storm surge different from high tide?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-sounding things are the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Cyclones cannot be predicted, so warnings are not useful.
misconceptions.why: Students think natural disasters are random and sudden.
misconceptions.fix: IMD tracks cyclones with satellites and radar and gives warnings days in advance.

probe.question: Can cyclones be forecast?

misconceptions.root_belief: nature cannot be predicted

misconceptions.statement: Earthquakes can be predicted exactly, so we only need to leave on time.
misconceptions.why: Weather forecasts for cyclones lead to assuming the same for quakes.
misconceptions.fix: Scientists cannot predict the exact time of earthquakes, so always be prepared to Drop, Cover and Hold On.

probe.question: Can we know when an earthquake will strike?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one hazard works for all

misconceptions.statement: An emergency kit only needs food.
misconceptions.why: Students think survival means eating.
misconceptions.fix: A kit also needs water, torch, radio, first-aid, medicines and a whistle.

probe.question: What should be in an emergency kit?

misconceptions.root_belief: one need covers everything

misconceptions.statement: It is fine to prepare the kit after the disaster begins.
misconceptions.why: Students feel preparation can wait until it is needed.
misconceptions.fix: Kits and papers should be ready before, in a waterproof bag, since there is no time during a disaster.

probe.question: When should the emergency kit be prepared?

misconceptions.root_belief: act only when it happens

misconceptions.statement: Messages forwarded on social media are as reliable as official warnings.
misconceptions.why: Forwards seem urgent and come from trusted contacts.
misconceptions.fix: Only trust IMD, disaster-management authorities and official announcements. Rumours can cause panic or wrong actions.

probe.question: A forwarded message says a flood is coming tonight. What should you do?

misconceptions.root_belief: messages from friends are reliable

misconceptions.statement: In a disaster, each family member should find safety on their own without any plan.
misconceptions.why: Students think everyone will manage to act instinctively.
misconceptions.fix: A family plan with a meeting point and contact person helps everyone reunite and avoid searching in danger.

probe.question: Why make a family plan?
probe.wrong_answer: Not needed; each person manages alone.

misconceptions.root_belief: everyone will just know what to do
